analysis.one_liner: Strips mortgage interest and depreciation tax breaks from investors owning 50+ single-family rentals.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Emilia Sykes and two cosponsors in October 2024, never got a hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would deny two large federal tax deductions — mortgage interest and depreciation — to any taxpayer owning 50 or more single-family rental homes, including properties held through related companies. The deductions would be restored only for the year such a home is sold to an individual buying it as their own residence or to a qualified affordable-housing nonprofit such as a community land trust. The goal is to make large-scale corporate ownership of single-family rentals less profitable and tilt the market toward owner-occupants and nonprofits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary renters and first-time homebuyers. Large corporate landlords lose a tax subsidy on every home beyond their 50th, which would either push them to sell homes to families or reduce the tax-advantaged edge they hold over individual buyers. Renters may also face less pressure from owners whose business model depends on cheap debt. Owner-occupant buyers would gain when large owners sell off homes.

how_it_helps.text: Denies the mortgage interest deduction to any taxpayer owning 50 or more single-family rental properties, with all commonly controlled companies counted as one owner, so large investors cannot split into small entities to escape the threshold.
Denies the depreciation deduction for those same large owners of single-family rental properties.

Restores both deductions in the year a property is sold — but only if the buyer is an individual using it as a principal residence or a qualified nonprofit dedicated to affordable housing, including community land trusts and land banks.
Excludes newly built housing and low-income housing tax credit properties from the definition, so the tax penalty targets buyers of existing homes rather than new construction.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporate investors in single-family rental homes, including institutional owners and syndicators, who would pay more federal tax on interest and lose depreciation write-offs on homes above their 50th property. Some of that cost could be passed to renters through higher rents or reduced maintenance on affected portfolios.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporate owners of single-family rentals

drawbacks.text: Supporters of large rental operators would argue the deductions they lose are the same deductions small landlords and other businesses get, and that removing them raises their cost of capital, which could be passed to tenants as higher rents or deferred maintenance.

The bill only counts owners above 50 properties, so the tax break stays intact for the many smaller investors who own the majority of single-family rentals — it targets the largest players but does not change the tax code for most landlords.

The tax cost falls only on debt-financed or depreciable activity; large all-cash owners of new construction, which the bill exempts, face little immediate pressure, so the effect on total corporate ownership could be gradual and indirect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted tax penalty aimed at a specific, growing business model — institutional ownership of single-family rental homes — with an escape valve that rewards selling to families or affordable-housing nonprofits. Its honest cost is uncertainty: removing deductions could raise costs for tenants if investors pass them through, and its scope covers only the largest owners while exempting new construction. It is a focused deterrent rather than a broad housing fix, and it never went anywhere, so its real-world tradeoffs were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes introduced the Stop Predatory Investing Act on October 4, 2024, with Reps. Dwight Evans and Nydia Velázquez as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day, which is where tax legislation must start.
The committee held no markup, and the House never took a vote on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, which kills bills that were not passed.
The bill had only two cosponsors besides its sponsor, all Democrats, giving it little cross-party support in a Republican-controlled House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate owners of single-family rentals keep the mortgage interest and depreciation deductions the bill would have taken away; no investor faced the new tax cost or pressure to sell to owner-occupants or nonprofits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate landlords keeping their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Emilia Sykes
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to deny interest and depreciation deductions to owners of 50 or more single-family rentals.

for.name: Reps. Dwight Evans and Nydia Velázquez
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Jason Smith, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor, which it could not do for a bill that cleared no committee.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats and the Republican-controlled House never acted on it; no Republican cosponsored.

industries.note: These investors would lose mortgage interest and depreciation deductions on every single-family rental they hold beyond their 50th, and could reclaim them only by selling to an owner-occupant family or an affordable-housing nonprofit. Their tax-advantaged edge over individual homebuyers was exactly what the bill targeted.

industries.industry: Residential real estate brokerage and sales
industries.note: If large landlords sold off homes to comply or exit, owner-occupant purchases would rise, potentially increasing transaction volume for brokers and lenders serving ordinary buyers.

industries.industry: Affordable-housing nonprofits, community land trusts, and land banks
industries.note: The bill restores the deductions for sales to qualified nonprofits — land trusts, land banks, resident-owned co-ops, and public housing agency subsidiaries — making such organizations favored buyers and opening a channel for converting rentals to permanently affordable housing.
